BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL REVENUE,EXEMPTION OP S100 ON ARTICLES ACQUIRED BY CANADIANS VISITING UNITED STATES- FORTY-EIGHT HOUR PROVISION,Mr. Speaker, I advised the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) that I desired to ask him whether he had any explanation to make concerning a report in the press indicating that importations of Canadian merchandise into the United States by tourists from that country to the value of $100 would be allowed to enter free only if such tourists had remained at least forty-eight hours in Canada; but that such regulation was subject to the proviso that if Canada waived the forty-eight hour provision with respect to her citizens visiting the United States and subsequently returning, a reciprocal arrangement would be made. It is a matter of such importance that I thought the minister might desire to make an explanation.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1145321,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.30.1.3,1938-04-25,396d7d47-d79c-4aea-bf33-18c3e7b199e3,ca.m.9501,Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of National Revenue):,Minister of National Revenue,QUESTIONS,NATIONAL REVENUE,EXEMPTION OP S100 ON ARTICLES ACQUIRED BY CANADIANS VISITING UNITED STATES- FORTY-EIGHT HOUR PROVISION,Mr. Speaker, a bill has passed the senate of the United States but has not reached any more advanced stage than that. Perhaps in view of the importance of the question I might read the part of the bill applicable to the matter in question:

That up to but not exceeding $100 in value of articles (including distilled spirits, wines and malt liquors aggregating not more than one wine gallon and including not more than one hundred cigars) acquired abroad by such residents of the United States as an incident of the foreign journey for personal or household
use or as souvenirs or curios, but not bought on commission or intended for sale, shall be free of duty:
column2: Provided further, that the

column1: secretary of the treasury may by special regulations or instruction, the application of which may be restricted to one or more individual ports of entry, provide that the exemption authorized by the preceding proviso shall be applied only to articles acquired abroad by a returning resident who has remained beyond the territorial limits of the United States for such period, not to exceed forty-eight hours, as the secretary may deem necessary at the specified port or ports to facilitate enforcement of the requirement that the exemption shall apply only to articles acquired as an incident of the foreign journey: Provided further, that the exemption authorized by the second preceding proviso shall apply only to articles declared in accordance with regulations to be prescribed by the secretary of the treasury by a returning resident who has not taken advantage of the said exemption within the thirty-day period immediately preceding his return to the United States: Provided further, that no such special regulation or instruction shall take effect until the lapse of ninety days after the date of such special regulation or instruction: And provided further, that section 37 of this act shall not take effect until ninety days after the effective date of this act: And provided further, that all articles exempted by this paragraph from the payment of duty shall also be exempt from the payment of any internal revenue taxes.

It will be noted that the section does not enact a forty-eight hour requirement, but it authorizes the secretary of the treasury to stipulate a forty-eight hour absence as a test of the bona fides of the declaration that the purchase was incidental to the visit abroad. 1145332,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.32.2,1938-04-25,4aa810f9-1c2b-42a6-95c4-d4e382d264a1,ca.m.6010,Hon. GROTE STIRLING (Yale):,,QUESTIONS,"DEFENCE EXPENDITURES AND VICTORIA, B.C., BYELECTION-AMENDMENT OF MR. STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"Before the house resolves itself into committee of supply there are certain observations I want to make with regard to the attitude taken by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) at the time of the Victoria byelection. Before proceeding I should like to express my regret, and the regret of those from British Columbia who are associated with me, at the untimely illness of Mr. Robert Mayhew, the member-elect. I did not meet Mr. Mayhew on that occasion, but I was much struck by the warmth of the appreciation which was expressed on all sides with regard to Mr. Mayhew, and we earnestly hope that he may make a speedy and complete recovery.

The attitude of the minister, to which I want to refer, is that he made an appeal, for partisan purposes, on the expenditure of money for the defence of this country, and particularly the expenditure on the Pacific

coast, added to the expenditure which would be undertaken by the government through the carrying out of the program outlined. The inference clearly was that the elector would do well to think deeply before he decided to vote against the government. There have been five ministers of national defence during the time I have occupied a seat in this house. None of the other four, so far as my knowledge goes, have made use of expenditures for the purpose of defence as an appeal for votes, and I think it is a deplorable thing that on this occasion the minister should have set such a precedent. The minister most clearly appealed for votes by submitting the expenditures of this government. Defence above all other things should be kept entirely free from partisanship. I believe there is a growing desire on the part of a considerable section of the general public that partisanship should be kept separate from expenditures of money in various departments. I think that a very great majority of the people consider that when we are discussing the defences of Canada expenditures of money certainly should not then be used as a basis for appeal.

Moreover, from the contact I had the privilege of having with the three branches of the service during the year I was minister, nothing was more clearly borne in on me than the fact that members of the services, departmental officials, were also desirous that questions of partisanship should not intrude themselves into their public work.

On November 18 the minister spoke to a theatre full of people in Victoria. I arrived in Victoria on the afternoon of the following day, and found that both the daily papers of the city contained a report of the minister's speech. Indeed so many of the observations of the Minister of National Defence were in inverted commas that I believe it is entirely probable that a statement was submitted to the press on behalf of the minister-and I am not suggesting the minister would be inclined to doubt the veracity of what appeared in the press.

There was a broadcast of proceedings at the meeting, and I met a considerable number of people who had either heard the minister in person or listened to him over the radio. There is no doubt therefore that the statement appearing in the Victoria Colonist is substantially accurate. I read now from the issue of November 19:

I have never sought to make the defence of Canada a political question and I do not intend to do so now,"" he declared. ""But I must tell you that the first week I was in office, I obtained a report on the condition of the three branches of the service-the navy, the army and the air force.
Defence Expenditures and By-Election

I found Canada lacked adequate forces to guarantee the neutrality in a war in which she did not wish to become a belligerent. Barracks, dockyards and other shore facilities of the naval service were antiquated and inadequate. The Esquimau naval magazine had been condemned in 1905 and nothing had been done about it,"" Mr. Mackenzie continued.

There were no anti-aircraft guns in Canada. The stock of field gun ammunition was only adequate for less than ninety minutes' firing. The existing field artillery was unsuitable for mechanical traction and was outranged from three to six thousand yards. Coast defences were obsolescent and defective. Firing from guns was restricted to prolong their lives.
There was no proper mechanization, no gas masks, no proper facilities for the manufacture of arms. The reorganization of the militia was recommended in 1932 and nothing had been done.""
Mr. Mackenzie further claimed that the twenty-three planes of the air force were all obsolescent. There was no supply of air bombs. No survey had been made for national defence, he stated.

He charged that the Conservative regime had wrecked the air force and had crippled the training of the militia, whose appropriation had been cut from 11 million dollars to 8-8 million dollars, a reduction of 25 per cent, while the air force had been cut from 7-4 million dollars to 1-7 million dollars, a decrease of 75 per cent.
Whatever the justification,"" he said, ""I ask you to remember the record of the Conservatives when they come to you preaching about national defence.""

Thereafter Mr. Mackenzie pointed out that the expenditure on Pacific coast defences under the regime of Mr. Bennett in 1935-36 totalled $1,916,116, while the appropriation for 1937-38 under the Liberal administration amounts to $8,163,188.

This is an expenditure for defence,"" he declared, ""which has not been equalled from the time of confederation. It must be borne in mind that the coast defence program cannot be completed until 1940. I ask you to remember what we are endeavouring to do, and I am taking this opportunity of requesting the electors of Victoria to approve the policy of defence of this coast when they go to the polls, November 29.""

There can be no doubt whatever, I believe, that that was a flagrant instance of an appeal for political purposes. It is so very different from the attitude adopted by the minister when his estimates were before the committee last year. On that occasion he fully realized that the official opposition indulged in no carping criticism. He knew the assistance given by the official opposition was an assistance to him at a time when he was not particularly comfortable, as he was expounding views which were not acceptable to a very considerable number of government supporters.

It will be noted also that at least some of the criticism he used was just as applicable to the administration prior to 1930 as it was to the subsequent one. But the great unfairness of the arguments he used is found in the fact that he made no reference to the tremendous change which has taken place throughout the world, a change-over from disarmament to rearmament. As a member of the League of Nations Canada was committed to disarmament. Her defence estimates were prepared year by year under an atmosphere of disarmament. She did not wish to increase her defence expenditures. Indeed, had she done so, it would not require a very vivid imagination to imagine the speeches which would have been made by the minister and his right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King). On account of the depression it was not possible during the disarmament period for the then government even to set aside the quantity of money required adequately to keep up the services as they then existed, and it was unfortunately necessary to cut the training of men. But to this fact the minister made no reference whatever.

There is nothing out of the common in the minister's argument; it is the typical Liberal argument: ""Use the facts which are convenient; make no reference to the facts which are not convenient, even though those facts are predominant."" I am reminded of another Liberal appeal for votes which was contained in the speech with which the right hon. leader of the Liberal party opened the campaign in 1935. He told of one of his famous soliloquies. He was standing on Wellington street. On his right front there rose a magnificent building, one erected by his administration and adapted to the peaceful purposes of labour and agriculture. On his left front there was rising the gaunt skeleton of another great structure built by the then administration at a cost of a million and a quarter dollars. For what purpose was it to be used? It was to be used by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. A great barracks was being erected in Calgary. Barracks for the use of the police and militia were going up from coast to coast, many of them being erected with money voted for relief. According to the Ottawa Citizen of the following day, the Prime Minister is reported as having said:

There are drill halls and armouries all over the country built at heavy cost"" he said. ""Why?"" ""It is to build up a great military force because all dictatorships demand force and the last word in dictatorship is the cannon and what comes out of the cannon.""

That was the view of the Prime Minister at the beginning of the 1935 campaign. Yet within eighteen months he and his Minister of National Defence were preparing estimates for submission to this house which were

$10,000,000 more than those submitted previously. The Minister of National Defence goes to Victoria and uses a diametrically opposite argument. The Prime Minister wished to paint us as war-like people.

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"As dictators. He claimed that we were making provision for cannons and for that which comes out of cannons, but when the increased estimates of 1937 were brought before this house it was found that they contained provision for cannons and that which comes out of cannons. On the one hand we have the leader of the Liberal party appealing for votes because we are making tremendous expenditures for military purposes. Then we have the Minister of National Defence, on the occasion of a by-election, trouncing us for not having made the necessary expenditures to keep up the defence of this country.

I should like to bring together the responsible facts of history which go to explain this tremendous change that has taken place. After the armistice the weary nations of the world met to lay down a platform of peace. They met to prepare a peace treaty and at the same time lay down the foundation of a noble structure for the preservation of peace. At the very first the idea of a league of nations suffered a heavy blow because of the withdrawal of a great nation which during the preparatory time had given its support but whose people were not ready to go any further.

The League of Nations came into being, and parallel with this fact, disarmament was imposed on Germany and her allies by our allies who themselves solemnly undertook to carry out voluntary disarmament. As time went on it became more and more difficult to bring a disarmament conference into being. There were wars and rumours of war. There was dissatisfaction because national boundaries had been drawn on the map with a pencil without sufficient notice being taken of racial distinctions and of the ideas which minorities have since shown that they believe in most strongly. Although the hope for a disarmament conference was dwindling, although such a conference was, shall we say, the first goal that the League of Nations attempted to reach, such a conference eventually did meet in February, 1932, when the delegates of sixty-one nations met in London to discuss disarmament. This conference was brought about because of the example set and the persuasion used by Great Britain. The conference had hardly met before it was realized that it was faced with the tremendous problem of

endeavouring to make agree two principles which were incompatible. The first principle was that the disarmament which had been imposed on Germany was necessary before voluntary disarmament could be undertaken by the other nations. The second principle, which was acceptable to many of the other nations, was that they could not agree to a basis of disarmament which would jeopardize their own conception of national security.

But the disarmament conference went on talking. Within a year Japan had withdrawn and eight months later Germany withdrew. Germany had come reluctantly to the conference and had taken the view all the way through that the one and only basis which could be accepted by her as the basis for disarmament on the part of those nations which agreed voluntarily to disarm was the basis which had been imposed on her and to which she had rigorously to conform because she was governed in her every act by disciplinary measures and inspections carried out by allied committees. Germany withdrew, but the disarmament conference went on talking. Indeed, it has not yet been officially terminated.

In March, 1935, Germany took another step; she threw over the military clauses of the Versailles treaty. Eight months later she repudiated Locarno. In October, 1935, Italy entered Abyssinia. In July, 1936, there was civil war in Spain. By the intrusion of European nations into this conflict, Europe was brought hazardously near to the brink of war. I cite these instances because I want to draw attention to the important fact that must be considered in connection with the armament of this or any other country. We must realize that we have passed from disarmament to rearmament. In making his political appeal the minister omitted any reference to that all-absorbing fact.

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"I have not found it in anything that I have read, but perhaps the minister will explain further.

In 1934 Great Britain could no longer keep her eyes closed to the fact that she had slipped to the position of a fifth rate power in the air. Germany was away to a flying start. Great Britain started feverishly to train pilots and mechanics, to build new factories and adapt old ones, to provide herself with the necessary materials and to make the tools and build the machinery necessary for the manufacture of engines and planes. She realized that she was away behind the race.
Dejcnce Expenditures and By-Election
Strive as she will, we still read from week to week in the press and hear it announced in the British house that she still realizes that she has not yet caught up.

It is not possible to name definitely the month in which disarmament gave place to rearmament. However, we can draw attention to the fact that the estimates for the Department of National Defence prepared prior to those of 1936 were prepared in an atmosphere of disarmament, whereas the subsequent estimates were prepared in an atmosphere of rearmament. It does not seem to me reasonable that a minister should go to a by-election and should preach the cause of political support citing as his reason for so doing the expenditure of money on national defence. Ever since the signing of the peace treaty, Great Britain had done all that she could to persuade and to lead the powers towards disarmament. She had made people in Great Britain, and indeed in the empire, extremely anxious as she reduced her navy in personnel and ships, as she reduced her little army, as she failed to replace her aeroplanes, and she did not even keep abreast of the tremendous scientific developments which were taking place with regard to the heavier-than-air machines. But she had pledged her word to disarm, and she was doing her best, whatever the spirit of the other nations might be, to carry out her undertaking.

Canada was in a similar position. She was a supporter of the League of Nations. The League of Nations had committed itself to disarmament. Great Britain had been preaching the word of disarmament and endeavouring to induce the nations to practise disarmament; she had hoped to lead the world to it. But she could not carry on further and see Germany overtake her in the air.

It is utterly improper in my opinion for a minister of the crown to use defence for the purposes of political appeal, and it is a reflection on public life for a minister to state a case with such unfairness as to omit reference to an overbearing and essential fact. Indeed, I do not think a public man will long enjoy the confidence of his public if he is known to be one who in stating an argument omits an essential fact On this occasion there can be no question that the minister made an appeal for votes by alluding to the expenditure of money for the defence of the Pacific coast, and not only the expenditure which was then going on, but the expenditure which would be carried on as the work proceeded which he had outlined. In my opinion this is such an unpleasant departure from the precedents of previous years that it is desirable to bring the matter before this house, and I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts):
That all the words after ""that"" in the said motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
In the opinion of this house, moneys appropriated by parliament for the defence of Canada should not be used, directly or indirectly, for political partisan purposes.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Grote Stirling,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4aa810f9-1c2b-42a6-95c4-d4e382d264a1&Language=E&Section=ALL

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"Mr. Speaker., in seconding this motion I should like to associate myself to the fullest possible extent with the remarks made by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) in connection with the by-election in Victoria, and I should like to draw the attention of the house to another occasion upon which the minister, or the department, or the government, or all of them, fell into the same deplorable state as they did in connection with the Victoria byelection, in that expenditures of public money in connection with a very important function of the government were made for partisan purposes. I refer to the method by which the Canadian contingent that was sent overseas to represent us at the coronation was selected.

As I have pointed out in this chamber before, Mr. Speaker, the coronation presented a golden opportunity for the Dominion of Canada to advertise its greatest product, its man power, at the greatest festival of empire that the world has ever seen. It was an occasion upon which the minister and the department and the government should have spared no pains to select from what I claim is the smartest body of men in uniform in the world to-day, the Canadian militia, a contingent that should be second to none. They should have been perfect in physique, perfect in drill, perfect in every respect in so far as what meets the eye may be concerned-because this was a parade, Mr Speaker. Our contingent, as did the other contingents, marched through the streets of London before a cloud of witnesses from all parts of the empire, and my complaint, and I am prepared to prove the facts on which it is based, is that in selecting the personnel of the Canadian contingent other considerations than those of merit entered into the mind of the minister. [DOT]
First of all I should like to refer to the King's Regulations and Orders for the Canadian Militia, which, by virtue of the Militia Act, have the force of statute law. Paragraph 429 reads as follows:
An officer is forbidden to write private letters to officials at National Defence headquarters, on official personal matters.
Attempts to obtain favourable consideration of any application by the use of outside in-

fluenee are forbidden, and, if resorted to, will be regarded as an admission on the part of the applicant that the case is not good on its merits, and it will be dealt with accordingly.

When an interview is asked for, or a letter written on behalf of an officer by any person other than himself, such application will be deemed to have been made at his suggestion, unless he can show to the satisfaction of the authorities that he has no knowledge, directly or indirectly, of such application.

Now I state as a fact, Mr. Speaker, that that paragraph was not adhered to in the selection of those who made up our Canadian contingent, and I submit, and I am prepared to prove it if given the opportunity, that political pressure was brought, and brought successfully, upon the department, with the result that the type of contingent that should have represented Canada did not go to London.

Just as one instance of what took place, let me say that I know of one entire corps which was. represented by only one officer. That is manifestly unfair on any basis of representation. The one officer who was chosen announced some four months before the selections of the contingent were made, shortly after it became known that a contingent was to go to the old country, that he had great pull with the government, and that he was going to London. And go he did. I can think of nothing that will operate more effectively to destroy the spirit which has always permeated the Canadian militia, the spirit which built up for Canadian troops a name that will live as long as history is written; and I challenge the minister to show that political influence was not brought to bear constantly in the selection of the Canadian contingent. As a result of that, because the smartest, the best drilled, the most perfect physical specimens that could be selected were not selected, many very unfortunate incidents followed.

There is, Mr. Speaker, a quaint old military custom, familiar to you, I have no doubt, familiar to all members of the house, certainly familiar to the minister, that when soldiers are on parade they march in step. I hold in my hand a photograph of the contingent taken on this side of the water as they approached the boat at Montreal. Let me make it quite clear at this point that I am aiming no criticism whatever at the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, none whatever at the representatives of the Canadian navy, and none at the band of the Royal Canadian regiment. My remarks are confined strictly to the militia contingent, composd, I believe, of 256 persons, thirty-two of whom were colonels or lieutenant-colonels and five of whom were privates. If the minister will take the trouble to scrutinize this photograph-and remember,

this was a public occasion-he will find, on looking at these persons representing the Canadian militia, that one soldier in the front rank is not in step with his leader, who is about ten feet distant.

That is of course bad drill, but it is bad business too. Going a little further, we come to the selection from a very large and important garrison centre, in which the local military authorities recommended an extremely smart officer who would have done great credit to them' as their representative. But he was overlooked, for very obvious reasons, and in his place was sent one who could only be described as the ward heeler supreme of that part of the country. He has been the bearer of the Liberal banner in every election since time immemorial, and is now enjoying a well-earned rest in a cushy patronage job which he derived from the present Liberal government of the province. I have here his picture taken on shipboard- and let me say, I bear no malice towards him in making these remarks. I make these remarks because I am particularly keen as a former militia man that the Canadian militia should be properly represented on important occasions of this sort, and I feel it a duty to the militia of the country to bring to light the manner in which patronage overrode all other considerations in the selection of this contingent. I leave it to the minister to look at this photograph I have here, showing some of the officers of the contingent that crossed the ocean-I leave it to him to decide whether this officer of whom I speak, who was chosen over the head of the local authorities, is a smart soldierly figure.

1145339,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.32.9,1938-04-25,d8b419fa-d0c7-4b4a-8319-d108a7fc73df,ca.m.3628,Mr. BETTS:,,QUESTIONS,DEFENCE EXPENDITURES AND VICTORIA, B.C., BYELECTION-AMENDMENT OF MR. STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"It is evidently a formal picture, because all the officers are wearing gloves and swords. The officer of whom I speak could not, by any standard, be described as either a good physical specimen or a good figure of an officer on parade. His head is resting on a splendidly developed double chin. He holds the rank of lieutenant-colonel, and large rolls of lieutenant-colonel are protruding over his Sam Browne belt.

That is not the type of officer that marched for the other dominions at his majesty's coronation. Words fail to describe the effect as I cast my eyes down his figure. His voluptuous calves are protruding from ill-fittings leggings, and his breeches-what shall I say of his breeches 1 They are tight where they should be loose and loose where they should be tight. They bring irresistibly to my mind that ditty immortalized by the troops
Defence Expenditures and By-Election
in France about ""those funny little pants that Maggie wore; they were baggy at the knees""-I won't continue, Mr. Speaker.

Let me make it clear, without any levity whatever, that that is not the type of officer who should have been selected to represent the Canadian militia at his majesty's coronation. And let me add that my criticisms have been echoed in every mess room, drill hall and canteen from Halifax to Vancouver.

Then, when we get to London, we find, in the picture I now hold in my hand, the guard moving to Buckingham palace, surely an important occasion. There they are moving along in fours and apparently the command ""Eyes left!"" has just been given; a compliment is being paid to somebody on the left of the parade. But one of the non-commissioned officers-a high-ranking one, you may be sure of that, because practically everybody in that contingent was high-ranking-is not thinking at all of the reason for the command; he is thinking of the girl he left behind him, or the big stoup of beer he will have at the barracks when he gets back. He is gazing straight ahead; he has missed out on his drill. Let me add that he is not one of the markers, and so his head and eyes should have been turned to the left. That is the sort of thing that happens when the canker of patronage eats into any department.

Taking up this souvenir book, which I imagine has had circulation 'all over the empire, we find a photograph of the Canadian contingent moving through Piccadilly circus, and at the head we see the band of the Royal Canadian regiment, moving as one man; properly covered off; all in step, just as smart as paint; and we cast our eyes to the left and find the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, a credit to their corps, their commissioner, and their dominion. Then behind that, there is a serpentine effect of troops wobbling about, not covered off, a bulge in the centre of the column-bad drill, almost no drill at all.

This was not an occasion on which to sound the party tocsin and raise the party standard and summon old Colonel Dropsy and Major Spavin from the Liberal committee rooms and send them overseas on a joy ride. The minister was not administering Liberal campaign funds; he was spending public money. He overlooked that, but the country has not overlooked it. Why did not the minister in making his selections pick fine upstanding fellows like himself who would make the girls catch their breath and say: ""Oh boy!"" when the troops marched by? I protest on behalf of the Canadian militia
and on behalf of the Canadian taxpayers that patronage was allowed to ruin this golden opportunity to advertise the Canadian militia in the heart of the empire.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Frederick Cronyn Betts,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=d8b419fa-d0c7-4b4a-8319-d108a7fc73df&Language=E&Section=ALL

IAN MACKENZIE (Minister of National Defence):,Minister of National Defence,QUESTIONS,DEFENCE EXPENDITURES AND VICTORIA, B.C., BYELECTION-AMENDMENT OF MR. STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"Mr. Speaker, I was

astounded upon hearing the address to which we have just listened, not only conceived but expressed and delivered in the worst taste I have ever seen displayed in the House of Commons of Canada. I desire in the first place to inform the hon. member that the Canadian coronation contingent was selected by a committee of the permanent force of Canada, and the recommendations came from the commanding officers of the units themselves. I have here the nominal roll of the men. A great number of them earned high decorations on the field of battle, and the remarks made by the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts) this afternoon are an insult to the reputation and military record of every single man of that contingent. Did hon. members notice the method of insinuation followed not only this afternoon but on a previous occasion? ""Yes, the mounted police were splendid."" So they were, but as the Canadian contingent, after receiving their decorations from the hand of His Majesty the King and Her Majesty the Queen, swung in column of four past Buckingham palace, I heard one of the highest military officers of Great Britain say, ""That was the finest marching by any part of the empire contingent.""

My hon. friend speaks of patronage. He knows as well as I do that in many cases men who were actually presidents of the Conservative organization were members of the coronation contingent, and as far as I am concerned that would certainly be no bar to their being selected. Several were so selected from within twenty miles of Ottawa, and in Winnipeg. But the hon. member now wishes to convey the impression that members of the contingent were selected because they were adherents of the Liberal party and supporters of Liberal policy. The opposition are saying that now for the first time, and they have now thrown this issue of defence into politics; it was done very definitely this afternoon. It was done in a gentlemanly way, as one would expect, by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), and now it has been done in another way by the hon. member who followed him. Let me inform my hon. friend that if he had been in charge of the selection of the Canadian contingent we should have seen something diabolical in the extreme, not something done honourably and

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"I have here one of the red tickets. I show it to the house. It is a military pass from military headquarters at Esquimalt entitling them to enter the premises. It has nothing whatever to do with any political organization. I also hold in my hand a membership ticket in the Victoria Liberal organization of last year. Is that a red ticket? No, it is white. But that is the way politics were introduced into that by-election, not by the Minister of National Defence, but by hon. gentlemen who sit opposite me this afternoon.
I have here several letters of thanks concerning the way these men were employed- letters not from political organizations, but from the legion and other ex-service bodies.

The leader of the opposition referred a few moments ago to an address I delivered during that campaign to the United Sendees Institute. Also the hon. member for Yale, speaking in Vancouver, I think on the day of the byelection or shortly aftenvards. made the statement that the Minister of National Defence had made a political speech to a military institute during the course of that by-election.

After it was announced that I was to speak in the Victoria by-election, and while I was crossing this continent en route to Victoria, a telegram was received by me from Major Crockett, secretary of the United Services Institute, as follows:

United Services Institute of Vancouver Island extend a cordial invitation to you to address them at time convenient to you during your visit to Victoria. If able to accept kindly let me know as soon as possible date and subject.
Major M. Kirkpatrick Crockett.

I demurred, as I thought such an address at that time might be misconstrued, as it has been this afternoon. I was assured by the officers of the institute that the meeting would be a private and confidential meeting, and so it was. I addressed that meeting, and there was not a single suggestion of political discussion during the whole course of my address. The other day I telegraphed to the officers of this institute, because I heard this question was coming up, and this is the reply I got. And let me say that the officers and members of that organization are not supporters of the party to which I belong. This is from a strong Conservative of Victoria who was present:

Have discussed matter of your wire with Major Kirkpatrick Crockett, secretary of the United Services Institution, and he is wiring you separately. Personally feel most indignant, and that all others of the one hundred present at meeting would feel likewise if they knew your courtesy and confidence had been abused. Your remarks were confined to facts of a confidential nature, without any possible political taint, and your audience was presented to you as being composed of officers and gentlemen. Would be ashamed to believe that anyone there present could state otherwise. General Austin, president, and Sir Percy Lake, mover of vote of thanks, agree with me.
The telegram received from Major Crockett, honorary secretary of the United Services Institution, was as follows:

Your address to United Services Institution of Vancouver Island was entirely military in character. Institution absolutely non-political and deals with service matters only. Your talk given at my invitation only after my assurance that meeting not open to press or non-members. Consensus of opinion is that you spoke as one officer to a group of brother officers and in confidence. President assured you that no publicity woidd be given meeting. Deeply resent any effort to misconstrue your kindness in addressing us.

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"I am quite sure of that. There was a misreport made by the Colonist which was not brought to the attention of my hon. friend; and I commended the Conservative party on both the first and second occasions on the support they gave the national defence estimates a year ago. I know where my hon. friend was misled; I have an idea who misinformed him both with reference to that meeting and the address delivered to the military institute. His allegations this afternoon are founded on misinformation that came from those in the city of Victoria who have been advising him; I could produce abundant evidence of that. I did criticize my hon. friends of the Canadian Commonwealth Federation party. I quoted what they said in this house last year, when they moved a vote of want of confidence on the estimates for national defence. Was it not fair for the Minister of National Defence, coming from the province of British Columbia, fighting a by-election in his own province, to explain to the people of Victoria what we were endeavouring to do last year when my hon. friends of the C.C.F. party moved a resolution of no confidence, which would have defeated this government, on the very issue I introduced into that by-election?

I make no apology for introducing the issue of national defence, and the people of Victoria to-day do not regret that defence was discussed. Then why all these post mortems and aftermaths, when the people of Victoria have decided this issue for all time? All the falsities and misstatements which have been brought to my hon. friends

opposite will not alter the decision and determination of the people of Victoria to see to it that the defences around that city are prosecuted with vigour, vision and firmness. We have had two addresses, one dealing with the by-election in Victoria and the other dealing with the Canadian coronation contingent. We have had one man insulting the uniforms of the Canadian army, with the other man relying on the tittle-tattle which has come to him possibly from citizens of Victoria in regard to declarations made by the Minister of National Defence. I have nothing to apologize for, nothing to retract and nothing to explain. At those meetings I commended the support of my hon. friends opposite and condemned the attitude of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and in regard to this question of defence I would pursue the same policy to-morrow. The Australian election not long ago was fought entirely on this issue of defence, and recent byelections in England and Scotland have been fought on the same issue. Sane defence should be one of the major policies of this country. Why should it be concealed from the people? Why this sinister assumption of secrecy at the present time in regard to general features of policy? Why? Because they lost a seat that had been theirs for thirty-one years; because the people of Victoria believed in the principles of this Liberal government. My hon. friends should take their defeat with patience and dignity. At this time they should not introduce a motion of no confidence in this government, in connection with a question already decided by the might and majesty of the public opinion of the good people of Victoria, British Columbia.

Cooperative Commonwealth Federation supporters in this house, and a motion which they moved. They did it, it is true-under protest from their officials, because they felt that we should have spent more money for the purposes of defence. We had to point out that money was not available, so long as people were suffering from the effects of drought in western Canada and the lack of food and shelter in other parts of the country. But the primary reason was that we were committed to a policy of disarmament, through the League of Nations-a policy which we carried out, and which we were pressed in this house to carry out, a policy which was constantly being brought to our attention, and which we were being urged to make effective.

I can recall in this very chamber one of the members then sitting to the left of Mr. Speaker, rising in his place in the house and asking how much it cost per annum, per month and per day to keep the destroyers we had in operation, in commission, and how far these expenditures would have gone towards supplying food and shelter to people in Canada. I only desire to point out that all of us have endeavoured to the best of our ability to support any proposal made by any government at any time for the defence of this country. It was not easy to remain silent last year, in view of the statements made by the Prime Minister at the opening of his campaign in Kingston, only a few short months before. It was not easy to do that. But we exercised that degree of self-restraint. Not one word of carping criticism was heard from anyone on this side of the house with respect to those expenditures. Why? Because we believed that on a question of defence we should not place personal and party considerations over a common purpose.

The minister says-and I am bound to accept his statement-that the administration of these moneys has not been made the subject of party or political considerations. I can only say to him-and I shall discuss it with him personally-that I have the names of many people who came to me in Victoria and told me the condition under which they would have to get employment would be to pay a dollar to join the Liberal association, and get the ticket which would enable them to work.

I do believe that so far as possible we should avoid the use of very strong terms in connection with matters of this kind. We should try to be as kindly as we can under the pro-

vocation which has been created. Certainly I do hope the Prime Minister will take the view that public money, expended for defence purposes, should not be utilized as purely partisan funds, and that those who pay the taxes after all should not be compelled to see that their taxes only go to provide employment for those who are the supporters of the government.

I can readily understand the many difficulties the government may have. I have been through them. I know that when the barracks were to be built at Calgary the same effort was made. I know that the names of prospective employees were placed in a hat, and the mayor drew out the names, regardless of political considerations, in order that employment might be given without discrimination, on the ground that it was public money. A large sum of public money was to be spent. The question as to political benefit could have arisen. There the difficulty was avoided when at the city hall the names were put into a hat and taken out by a disinterested party. That was the fair way to do it, it seems to me.

I do know this that I saw something of the work that was going on in Esqui-malt. I came in contact with many people, and they made the same complaint, that they could not find employment unless they had the approval of the Liberal party. I do not know that the Liberal government took the view that that was unsound.

that now prevail in the world. We have not changed our policy of disarmament to one of rearmament merely because we are an isolated community; we did it because all the world has made that change. Those who are familiar with the history of the early days of our confederation will remember that at that time the nations of the world were arming. Germany in particular was arming, for the war of 1870 was not far off and France and the other countries of Europe were doing likewise. With a coast line both east and west and with trade to protect we are endeavouring by some united action to attain a given end.

I do hope the Prime Minister will find it possible to make a statement that will not induce the people to conclude that when their taxes are paid they can be made available only to providing work for those who support the government of the day. I do hope that that difficulty, which is a very real one in many communities, will disappear and that moneys voted by parliament for the defence of Canada will not be utilized for purely political partisan purposes.

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"Yes, on one

occasion, but it gave rise to so much misunderstanding thereafter that I have thought it would be desirable at the moment to make perfectly clear just when that course might be followed without the possibility of its purpose being misconstrued; in other words when it would be appropriate.
Bourinot in his Parliamentary Procedure has the following at page 424:

An amendment moved to the motion to go into committee of supply (or ways and means) does not necessarily involve want of confidence in the administration. When such an amendment simply affirms a general principle, or sets forth a public grievance, and does not directly or impliedly challenge the conduct or policy of the government, it is not, in a parliamentary sense, a motion of want of confidence, and consequently cases often occur of the government agreeing to the passage of such motions.

I would say that we can only judge as to whether this amendment does impliedly attack the government by the speech made by the hon. member who moved it. I think hon. members will agree that the hon. gentleman's speech was in the nature of a direct attack upon the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie), an attack upon his attitude in discussing defence estimates at a by-election in Victoria; and if the government were to accept this amendment to the motion to go into supply, having regard to the speech which the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) has just made, it would be regarded as an expression of want of confidence in the government and in the minister in particular. In those circumstances I do not think the government can accept the amendment of my hon. friend moved as it is an amendment to the motion for the house to go into committee of supply. On the other hand, I have no hesitation whatever in saying that apart from the implication referred to, the government is wholly in accord with the substance of the amendment and the principle as set forth in the amendment, namely, that moneys appropriated by parliament for any purpose whatsoever should not directly or indirectly be made to serve political partisan ends.

My right hon. friend (Mr. Bennett) says that the taxpayers will resent very strongly the idea that public moneys should be used for the purpose of serving political partisan ends. Well, he has good reason to know that that is true because in the last campaign, as I recall it, he did not confine his urging of public expenditures to one particular coast but started at one coast and went clear across the country from coast to coast advocating all along the way the expenditures of public moneys for purposes that would serve political

partisan ends. And he got his answer direct from the electorate. They made it very plain that they strongly resented the leader of a political party seeking -to win power by promising large expenditures of public moneys in the several constituencies in which he was seeking to elect his candidates.

What has been the position in Victoria? Holding the view that the electorate does resent the use of public moneys for political partisan ends, the electors of Victoria quite evidently did not regard the Minister of National Defence in what he was saying as seeking in any way to bribe the electorate. They understood perfectly well that he was defending one of the policies of the government, a policy which, in view of the attitude taken by the supporters of one of the candidates in that election, required to be defended at the instance of the minister. It must not be forgotten that in the by-election at Victoria there were three candidates. There was not Only the Liberal candidate, but there was the candidate of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and the candidate of the Conservative party, and it appeared from the results, as we assumed at the time, that the candidate of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation was a much stronger candidate than that of the Conservative party.

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"And that lends point to what I am saying at the moment. The government realized in fighting the byelection at Victoria that it had to make perfectly clear what its position was in regard to expenditures on defence. The Cooperative Commonwealth Federation members in this house had moved a want of confidence motion against the administration on the score of its defence expenditures. This apart from all else made it necessary for the minister to make the explanation in detail which he did.

May I say that I agree very largely with what the hon. member for Yale has said, and also with what the right hon. leader of the opposition has said, when they urged that matters of defence and, I would add, matters that relate to foreign policy should not become unnecessarily controversial if that can be avoided, or be made too much an occasion for discussion in political campaigns. I wish we could make it a general rule that that view

would be observed. Unfortunately it is only too true that there has scarcely been a byelection or a general election in some of the provinces of this dominion in which the question of defence has not been made a very live issue in the campaign, and the government has had to put forward in the clearest terms its policy and the reasons underlying it.

The hon. member (Mr. Stirling) has spoken about the difference between disarmament and rearmament. I agree with him that there was a period of disarmament which unquestionably had its influence upon the policies of the government. He says that it influenced the conduct of his government, and I am prepared to accept that statement; but I am not prepared to accept the view that the government of which he was a member was influenced by both policies. Defence Expenditures and By-Election

which was conducted there by the supporters of the government. The minister has denied that he was in any way implicated in the promises and insinuations made and I accept his statement, but I would nevertheless point out that the canvassers on the government side invariably endeavoured to persuade the electors that it would be very much better to have a Liberal member returned to this parliament because he could speak for Victoria when these large expenditures were about to be made. That, it seems to me, is on all fours with the type of campaigning which was carried on in Montreal where responsible ministers of the crown made the statement that the hole on Dorchester street would be filled by a railway, which though owned by the government is managed by an independent board. That kind of campaigning reflects not only upon the government, but upon the entire institution of parliament.

The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) referred to the fact that it was necessary to defend the government's position owing to the attacks that were made last year upon the estimates by the group with which I am associated. Last year our attack was centred largely around the point of view that the government, which could not find money for public works to alleviate unemployment, could find money for large military expenditures; and at Victoria, last autumn, our attack upon the defence proposals was centred very largely around the point that the Dominion of Canada was at that time permitting the export in vast quantities of scrap iron, nickel, copper, and other basic war materials to the nation which was clearly indicated by the government speakers as being the potential enemy of Canada in the future, or the country from which we might some time expect an attack. The nation was never named; but it was clear to anyone who heard, for example, the Reverend Clem. Davis, to whom reference has been made, speaking over the air, that that was the inference the electors should take from the statements of Liberal speakers. And it was very largely, as the records will show, on the grounds I have indicated that we attacked the defence proposals which were being advocated by the minister and the Liberal party.

In that by-election, as in previous general elections and by-elections, certain specific promises were made on behalf of the government. In Victoria the people were told to vote for the Liberal candidate, not only for the defence of the Pacific coast, but for the institution of unemployment insurance. "" Vote for Mayhew and unemployment insurance""
was the slogan of speakers throughout the city during the by-election. To-day we seem to be a long way from the enactment of an unemployment insurance measure.

While I am speaking of the Victoria by-election, may I refer to some others also? I have referred to the one in Montreal. Out in East Edmonton the same kind of campaigning was carried on. National control of currency and credit, old age pensions at fifty-eight, I think it was, or was it sixty?

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"The amendment before the house involves, first, the question whether or not the defence works being carried on in and around the city of Victoria at the time of the recent byelections were used for the purpose of securing Liberal preferment in that election. The charge is clear-cut and well defined, namely, that the man who got employment in that work had first to secure a Liberal ticket. It has now been changed a little bit from the charge that was made in the by-election itself. It is now said that you had to get a membership ticket from the Liberal party before you could get the red ticket which permitted entry into the various areas where defence works were being developed.

The investigation which was carried on during the by-election disclosed that every man working in Victoria and vicinity had to obtain that red ticket before the contractor was permitted to employ him. It was not

a membership ticket in the Liberal association, but a military pass issued by the assistant adjutant-general and quartermaster-general of military district No. 11 at Work Point. This matter was clearly laid before the electorate during that by-election, as everyone knows who participated in it. And the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) fully explained to the electors in Victoria that work of the nature of that carried on at Albert Head was necessarily surrounded with a certain measure of secrecy. It was therefore decided that as far as possible only men who had taken the oath of allegiance to serve his majesty in the armed forces of the country should be permitted on the premises. Employment was actually restricted to exservice men and members of the non-permanent militia. Word to this effect was circulated among the militia units and the exservice men's clubs.

A surprising thing about this charge is found in the proportion of the number of men employed to the number of electors in Victoria. I want to congratulate my friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation on the fact that notwithstanding the pitiful rout which that party suffered during the general election they returned to the fight in Victoria, and increased the vote of their candidate by something like 390. I venture to think that was due to the splendid platform ability of the hon. member who has just preceded me (Mr. Coldwell). I also want to congratulate the Conservative party, because with a very bad candidate and after a very hard trip all the way from Halifax the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) took up what was recognized as almost a forlorn hope and succeeded in increasing the vote of the Conservative candidate over the vote secured by the very much beloved and lamented late Doctor Tolmie in Victoria by some 1,700 votes. With such success coming to both Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and the Conservative party it would seem that the Liberals were in a desperate plight and might in their weakness feel it necessary to resort to some such tactics as have been charged. But for some reason or another the Liberal party, after taking third place in the previous election, was successful in changing that to first place with an increase of, not 390 votes or 1,700, but three thousand and some odd hundreds. What part could the red ticket or the Liberal association membership ticket have played in that, the total number of men employed on the defence works at that time being 291? And with the exception of fifteen key men every one of

those was a returned man or a member of the militia and recommended by branches of the Canadian Legion, the Army and Navy Veterans, the Imperial Veterans, or the officers commanding the Canadian Scottish, the fifth C.G.A., the Army Service Corps, the Seventeenth Fortress Company and the Royal Canadian Naval Veterans Reserve.

The best test of the virtue of the charge made here to-day is found in the vote of the electors, because they voted upon these very facts; for all the issues raised in the charges made in supporting this resolution were raised in the Victoria by-election. If there is one group of men who more than any other, would resent the type of thing charged here it would be the returned men in the city of Victoria. But on November 11 the Imperial Veterans' Association, Victoria and district branch, wrote to the Hon. Ian Mackenzie, M.P., Minister of National Defence, Ottawa, as follows:
Dear Sir:
At an executive meeting of above association the following resolution was passed, and I am hereby authorized to send a copy on to you.

Whereas the Department of National Defence in respect to the Albert Head project have laid down definite policy of allocation of employment re ex-service men, we the executive of the Imperial Veterans' Association of Victoria and district desire to go on record that we endorse the same and consider it of unquestioned fairness.""
I am, sir, your obedient servant,
T. Miller,
Secretary.
That was before the election. After the election the minister received from the Canadian Legion of the British Empire Service League district council, Victoria, B.C., the following:
Dear Mr. Mackenzie:

At a meeting of the Victoria and district council, Canadian legion, British Empire Service League, held a few nights ago, I was instructed to convey to you the council's heartiest congratulations and best thanks on the arrangements made between your department, the Northern Construction Company and the Employment Service of Canada in so far as the employment of ex-service men on the Albert Head project is concerned.

Warm appreciation was voiced by the delegates present, and the hope expressed that the same arrangements will be as amicably arranged in any future contracts that may be entered into between your department and other companies.
From the first battalion, Canadian Scottish regiment, Victoria, came this letter, addressed to the Minister of National Defence:
I wish to take this opportunity, on behalf of my battalion and myself, of expressing

appreciation of the manner in which employment of labour has been carried out in the defence works at Albert Head. The giving preference to employment of returned soldiers and serving members of the non-permanent active militia is eminently fair, and will do much towards the building up of the necessary defence forces.
May I express the hope that this policy will be continued in the further works that are now under consideration.
Respectfully yours,
J. R. Kingham, Lt.-Col.,
Officer commanding.

I want to come now to the other issue that was raised by the leader of the opposition in his own particular way, and I ask hon. members to remember that according to the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) this amendment is based upon the assumption that men seeking votes from the electors for themselves or their party candidates should stand upon the highest ethical grounds of truth in stating facts to the public. As we saw that issue in Victoria, a world situation developed in which there was a possibility not merely of increased friendship between the British and United States governments but also of increased friendship and understanding between the people of Great Britain and the nations of the British Empire and the people of the great republic to our south. Some discussions had taken place between Great Britain and the United States indicating a desire on the part of both governments to formulate and consummate a new trade agreement between those two great countries. As soon as that information was made public, it was assumed by the leader of the opposition and his party that no such agreement could be formulated or consummated without sacrificing the empire trade agreements or some portion of them, and that no possible compensation could be secured by Canada that would permit her to authorize any variation or change in those agreements. The right hon. gentleman had a direct appeal to make to the fears of the lumbering interests, the fruit interests and the fishing interests of that great province on the Pacific coast. He not only charged this government with bringing obsolete guns from Halifax to defend the Pacific coast; he deliberately charged this government with a ready willingness to sacrifice not only the interests of the empire but the interests of the Do-

minion of Canada in a futile attempt to appease the people of the United States. Listen to how far he went. He said:
I would ask you people of this city to have the government of Canada say, before Saturday night-
That was the night of the election.
-whether or not the preferences on lumber are to go. That is the issue in this by-election. I know your government has agreed-
Now, notice the way in which the reporter of his own press carried that message to the people who did not hear it on the radio or who were not at the meeting. He said:
I know your government has agreed,"" and there Mr. Bennett halted, leaving the inference the government has already committed itself to certain things concerning the lumber exports of Canada.

I know your government has agreed,'' and then an inferential pause; but the reporter of the Conservative press did not take any chances on any unintelligent individual interpreting the meaning of that pause. He supplied what he at least thought the right hon. gentleman intended to convey.

Continuing, he declared: ""Let this country know that this matter has been settled in a corner; that it has been discussed in cabinet. Never in my life have I been so concerned over public matters as this and it needs no prophet to see where it is all going to meet. It is an hypocrisy to say that this thing is being done in the sacred name of peace.""

Well, Mr. Speaker, on the same day that this extraordinary statement was reported in the press of Vancouver and Victoria messages came through from Australia in quite a different tone. The Vancouver Province carried the following report from Sydney:

Grim warning of Australia's dangers in the event of war, and a strong plea for British empire understanding with the United States were made by Prime Minister Lyons in a recent speech on the Pacific situation.
Mr. Lyons stressed the dangers to Australian trade routes to-day and envisaged the possibilities of a blockade of Australia.

We must foster the friendship and cooperation of other nations desirous of following the path of peace,"" said Mr. Lyons, ""and in this regard the Australian government will cooperate in seeking a cordial political and economic understanding betwen the British Empire and the United States.
We believe that the British Empire working in close cooperation with the United States can be an irresistible force of reason and conciliation.

In the face of realities which every day grow more ghastly this great nation has been obliged to jettison a noble experiment and throw in the lot of her people with others who seek not for aggression but for peace.
[Mr. McGeer.l

Any policy designed to guarantee the security of Australia must be one of cooperation in trade and defence with other members of the British Empire, and a political and economic understanding with the United States.""

That was the very program, both in the matter of defence and in the matter of trade agreements which were to be considered between Great Britain and the United States, as we placed them in the issues of the byelection, to be voted upon by the electors in one of the most conservative and British cities in the whole of Canada. It was not a red ticket, a Liberal ticket, the misuse of public funds, the abuse of privilege by the Minister of National Defence, or a wrong act by any of the supporters of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Mayhew) and the government which won so magnificent a majority. It was a clear presentation of the real issues involved. What I, and other persons engaged in the election, asked the electors to decide in casting their ballots was, first: Are you in favour of the defence program and its extension by the government, so far as the Pacific coast is concerned and, second, are you in favour of the government of Canada cooperating with Great Britain and other nations of the British Empire in helping to bring about a reasonable understanding between the people of the British Empire and those of the United States? Upon those issues they voted.

Some little word has been said that it was unfair to criticize the policy of the late government in matters of defence, because they were acting in league with a world program designed to create disarmament. No league of nations conference ever considered there was any necessity for disarmament in Canada, became Canada had never armed. The remarks of the right hon. the leader of the opposition quoted recently in Liberty magazine make that more than clear. The editor states that two years ago Liberty had the privilege of publishing the editorial, which I shall quote, by ""the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, former Prime Minister of Canada."" So that he was writing this, not when he was in power, but when he sat in the cool, quiet shades of opposition, with all the time required for reflection. Here is his statement as to a national defence policy for the protection of the dominion;

We have subscribed lightly to international covenants because others were doing so. If we had so much as hesitated to sign on the dotted line we would have gravely charged ourselves with delaying the millenium. We know now that these international emotional cloudbursts have little meaning. We cannot act alone; but we can, in association with others having similar aspirations and ideals,
Defence Expenditures and By-Election
endeavour to give international contracts of the future some basis of reality. The problem of protection from external aggression is one that Canada has never seriously faced.

The issue we raised in that by-election was whether or not we should now face the issue as Canadian people, and whether or not we would secure from a national government a real program of Pacific defence which would recognize this dominion as a Pacific ocean nation. That was the issue involved in the by-election. I cannot see that that is anything but right and proper. Surely the people of Victoria and Vancouver, and of British Columbia generally, have the right to say whether, after full and open discussion, they approve the new policy inaugurated by this government of facing squarely within the means: of the country the development of a defence system on the Pacific coast which will give at least some measure of security from sporadic raiding, should conflict break out among the larger powers.

This charge is just as silly and absurd as was the plea made by the leader of the opposition. If this same charge, supported by the meagre facts upon which it rests, were submitted to the electors of Victoria tomorrow, the majority secured by the Liberal party in the by-election would be overwhelmingly increased. I doubt whether this would do any great good to the Minister of National Defence. It can hardly add to his popularity on the Pacific coast, because that popularity is just about at the highest point it can reach.

STIRLING TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE",,"Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for me to refrain from speaking for a few moments in answer to the observations of the hon. member for London (Mr. Betts). He has assumed the liberty of criticizing severely the manner in which the contingent representing Canada at the coronation was chosen. I believe he has used language which reflects unfairly not only upon the government but upon the stamp and type of many of the splendid men who composed that contingent. I know nothing about how that contingent was chosen, generally, but I do know something about the choice made in my constituency. I know that there the military people chose a man who had a splendid record overseas, one who was a smart and able soldier and who was not at that time or never has been an officer.
It has been my privilege to serve overseas in the ranks of the Canadian expeditionary force, and I believe I can speak with some authority with respect to an able and smart

non-commissioned officer. He was a representative officer and he honoured us by being in that contingent. He was well thought of and a highly esteemed and capable noncommissioned officer. I want to make this clear for his sake so that the people of my town will know that the choice of this man was made entirely by his comrades and officers in his own regiment. The selection was made utterly free of any influence of any kind. I had nothing to do, either directly or indirectly, with that selection.

This man went over there as a representative of his regiment. He glories in the fact that he was so chosen and he considers it an honour. Those who are dear to him also consider it an honour that he was so chosen to represent the regiment of which he was a member. I think it is unfortunate that it should be intimated that this choice was political. I realize that the hon. member does not single out this or that regiment, and I do not profess to speak in connection with the general selection. The minister and those responsible are well able to answer for themselves. However, in honour of the type of man I have referred to, in honour of the officers and men of his regiment who selected him, I think I should say these words. If they disagree in any way they will let it be known. In justice to them, I think the words I have said should be said.

May I add just one more word before I sit down? I am learning things from day to day and from week to week by listening to the debates in this chamber and observing the methods resorted to in connection with what might be termed parliamentary tactics or strategy. If there was anything censorable done in Victoria-as far as I know there was not-if national defence has been used for political purposes, then I think it is fair to say that because of the form of the motion that has been made an attempt is being made to force me to take a stand which indicates that I am approving of our defence policies being injected into political warfare. As has been pointed out by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), with the present wording of the motion I must choose between censoring the government-this amendment is equivalent to a motion of want of confidence-and appearing to support something that I naturally do not wish to support. Practically all hon. members agree that we do not want our national defence policies to be degraded to the extent that politics are played in connection therewith.

I wish merely to record my attitude on this matter. I think hon. members of the opposition generally and the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), who moved the amendment, would have been more fair to the public and would have put this issue more clearly before the house if they had stated that this motion was intended to censor the present government for playing politics in connection with the national defence policies of Canada. I do not believe that has been done. I believe they have subtly and cunningly injected this in the amendment they have put before us. Naturally I am voting against it because I believe the Prime Minister, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) and their colleagues have scrupulously tried to avoid mixing up our national defence policies with politics.

My belief is that the time of this house could be better employed than in setting up straw men and burning them down with fiery rhetoric. I had hoped that for the rest of the session wr would be through with fiddling and would perhaps devote more time to the fire protection of our Canadian Rome, which many of us think is burning.

When responsible members of this or other legislative bodies waste their time in this sort of thing, irreparable damage is done to the institutions of democracy. To-day's Hansard may cause a few chuckles in the odd militia mess, a few grins in party gatherings, but it will surely disgust the majority of ordinary people. I do not want to say anything more lest I condemn myself by my own remarks, but I do want to draw attention to what to my mind, and to the minds of the people of my constituency, has been a wasted afternoon.

Mr. CHURCH; I can see no reason why Ontario should not be given equal treatment with the rest of Canada in this matter. Why

is this province not entitled to ice-breakers? In some of the municipalities bordering on the chain of inland lakes there are many public utilities that cannot operate in winter except under favourable conditions. There is a large vote for work of this kind in connection with Hudson bay, work that is scarcely necessary, whereas last winter the people of Ontario were faced with a serious state of affairs on the Niagara river where public utilities might in one half hour have been closed down, disrupting transportation and water services. I say that Ontario, in the matter of ice-breakers, is entitled to the same consideration which has been shown to other parts of Canada that have been favoured in this respect since confederation. Niagara river is navigable in part and there is an investment there of some $60,000,000, but when an ice-breaker is needed it is not available. I understand that an application was made to Toronto for assistance but without success, and had it not been for a favourable wind coming along at the right time a r umber of power companies would have been swept away and various utilities ruined for want of an ice-breaker. Under this item I can see no reason whatever why Ontario should not be given equal treatment with other parts of Canada. The province does not get very much money for harbours, and I submit that the department should give it some consideration.

1145490,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.21,1938-04-25,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Transport,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,This vote covers services on the great lakes of the type my hon. friend mentions. For instance, we have two large boats with headquarters at the Parry Sound agency, and we contract for ice-breaking at the head of the lakes, using private boats for the purpose. The duty of this department, however, is to maintain navigation, and Niagara river is not navigable. The department has spent some $130,000,000 in providing navigation facilities for the Niagara escarpment by means of the Welland canal. We maintain a boat at Kingston and boats on the Trent canal, and in a general way we have attempted to give Ontario just as good service in the maintenance of navigation as we provide in the province of Quebec and the maritimes. I think we have succeeded reasonably well in that endeavour, for we have always been able to open the lakes at the same time as the St. Lawrence.

there are other bridges which might have been destroyed in the same way as the ""Honeymoon"" bridge; there are steamer landings at Queen-ston, Lewiston and Niagara that have been carried away, and had there been an icebreaker in the river below these points this might not have happened. In my opinion the government should not regard the supplying of ice-breakers as pertaining entirely to navigation. I repeat, we do provide exactly the same type of service throughout the waterway system in Ontario that we provide in the province of Quebec and the maritimes.
