1145510,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.41,1938-04-25,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,Under this item an important principle is involved; that is the principle of what Canada is doing at the present time

to create employment. This empire came into being by the sea. Canada has a large number of men out of work, many of them on the dole. Why does the minister not say to these young men-it may be in conjunction with the Minister of National Defence

Do you want to join in a volunteer navy with pay? Canada excels in all kinds of aquatic sports. At the time of the Gordon expedition up the Nile they had to appeal to Canadians to man the boats. There are now two schools of navigation, one at Lunenburg and one at Queen's university. There are thousands of young Canadians who would go to such a school, take up shipping and navigation if they could, and qualify for the merchant marine, which is the back-bone of the British navy. But this government sold a lot of merchant marine ships for a song, and the empire has 2,000 fewer merchant ships to-day than it had in 1914.

The minister, in association with those of other departments, should come along with a forward educational training policy for the great lakes and the seaboard, establish these schools throughout Canada where needed, and give free tuition for the navy. At present there is one in Lunenburg and another meets for a short time at Queen's. Why are not these schools established in connection with the other universities of the dominion, and on the same scale as the militia for the army? There are hundreds of young men in the canoe clubs, rowing clubs and yacht clubs of the country. This empire came into being by the sea and without it the empire would not last. We should train men for the British fleet and merchant marine. The government feels that adequate armaments are necessary, but armaments without adequate man power are useless. The minister could do a great deal to aid unemployment among the youth of our dominion, many of whom go down to the waterfront in the spring of the year in order to look for something to do on the ships. A survey and recruiting volunteer system should be established. As hon. members know, conditions in the merchant marine to-day in Canada.are not what they should be, from the standpoint of health as well as in other ways, and as a result the young people do not go in for that branch of the service. To-day our navy depends upon foreign petrol and not coal for its motive power. If we are to continue in the British Empire the time has come for us to do something in regard to our naval strength, not only in connection with merchant shipping but in relation to other
Supply-Transport-Miscellaneous
branches of marine work, and give active aid to the British navy and merchant marine. Where are the navy leaguers?

The Department of Marine has been in existence since confederation, largely for the benefit of the maritime provinces. It has not done very much for the great lakes or for the development of the youth of Canada for sailors or for that fine arm of the British forces. I know of no country that can produce better seamen, not only for the merchant marine but for other ships, and also cadets for officers than Canada, but our young men have no opportunity to become trained for that work. It is true that there are a couple of schools each receiving a grant of $600, but I think the time has come for the government to consider a proper, adequate, national policy. We are a maritime, nautical people, or should be. We have our great coast lines and this magnificent chain of lakes, and $250,000,000 invested in canals. Look at what they are doing in Detroit in the war marine department and all down the great lakes on the other side! We are asleep on this side of the border. Such a policy would provide employment for thousands of young people and give them a calling, but instead we simply vote the same amount year after year. Hundreds of 3'ouths leaving our high schools cannot find work. They belong to these aquatic clubs from Vancouver to Halifax. If they had someone to give them a lead; if there was a forward policy provided by the government, it would mean a great deal not only in the way of employment but also in the defence of Canada and the British Empire. Look at what New Zealand and Australia are doing! W7e had some merchant marine ships owned by the government which were sold for a mere pittance; ten ships sold for about $500,000, and now ships are badly needed to carry food to the old country in time of emergency. We have only a couple of schools of this kind, which are attended by very few people. I do not know how many days the schools last; I understand they are only seasonal, and I think this whole matter should be considered in a bigger, broader spirit by the government if we are to have any sort of defence on our sea coasts and great lakes. We should take a leaf out of the book of our sister dominions and aid the freedom of the seas by providing men and cadets.

The section reads:
Every British subject who-
(1) served as a master or mate of a foreign-going or home-trade sailing ship of over 75 tons, gross tonnage, before the first day of January, one thousand nine hundred and thirty-one-

1145536,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.67,1938-04-25,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,We had the act before us, as it came from England, and as it had been adopted by the imperial parliament and by the parliaments of the several dominions. There arose in every country, as there does in this, the question of those who have served in a capacity seeking recognition of that service in terms of their then employment. For instance, when the lawyers of the country first set up their organizations it was sometimes provided that if a man had been practising law for a period of years he might be entered on the register. That was so in the Northwest Territories, when we first organized the law society. Provisions were made in the same way with respect to certain types of dentists.

With respect to masters and mates, to which this is limited, there had to be evidence that during a period of ten years preceding the date of the application, which could not be made after 1931-and subsequently extended to 1936-they had actually served-and the word that governs is ""served""-either as masters or mates. If they had served as masters for a period of years, it was assumed that they were qualified to serve as such in a ship of seventy-five tons and therefore they got a certificate of service. If they had served as mates, it was assumed that they had gone through the various grades that qualified them to serve as mates; otherwise they would not be employed as such. They also got certificates of service.

I must say that when the act was under consideration by the former government, this was one of the clauses which gave me great concern. The minister by his amending legislation extended the time from 1931 to 1936. It is true the act was not in force until it was proclaimed and it was not proclaimed during the whole of those five years. Nevertheless, the time was extended. The minister has pointed out that no great hardship could possibly arise, although I have always had grave doubts about this type of legislation.

It cannot affect the evil the hon. member for Nanaimo has referred to; for the simple and obvious reason that if a man had served as a master for twelve months he must have been qualified to act as such. If he was not qualified, he had no right to be a master. It is idle to think that he got a certificate of service without having had a seaman's experience. He had risen to the rank of master or mate, and having risen to that rank he received a certificate saying that he had served and as such was recognized. I may say to the hon. member for Nanaimo that it
-Miscellaneous
Supply-Transport

is a recognition of having attained a position, the duties of which he is fulfilling. A man should be entitled to a certificate of service indicating that he had satisfactorily discharged his duties either as mate or master. On that basis he should get a certificate, and not otherwise.

1145544,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.75,1938-04-25,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,"Ever since I have been a member of parliament I have been directing the attention of this committee to the discrimination that exists in connection with the life-saving service of this country. If there is one item that should not be reduced, it is this one. The vote was $48,000 last year and it has been reduced to $47,000. Only a small amount of this vote is used in connection with life-saving. As will be seen from the details, an amount of $30,080 is provided for temporary assistance; an amount of $9,925 is provided for board-no life-saving there- an amount of $5,845 is provided for supplies and repairs, and an amount of $550 is provided for sundries. There is not much lifesaving in all this.

Toronto is spending twice the amount of this vote on life-saving services. That city has to do practically all the life-saving work needed in central Ontario. I acted for the city as chairman of the harbour board when we took over the life-saving service from the former Minister of Marine and Fisheries, Mr. Hazen. On lake Ontario from Toronto and Hamilton to Cobourg there are only two lifeboats built in 1915, and I doubt if you could get them out of their sheds if anyone was in danger of being drowned. The city of Toronto spent about $35,000,000 on its harbour and the life-saving station at Toronto has to do federal government work. Some $47,000 is provided for this work in the maritime provinces and I doubt if it is half enough. Toronto spends $52,340 for maintenance and equipment, and $20,795 for materials and supplies. I am not objecting to other places getting lifesaving services, my argument is that there should be an equality of service and treatment all along this magnificent stretch of navigable waters from the gulf of St. Lawrence, through the St. Lawrence river and our great lakes.
Supply-Transport-Life Saving Service

What are the facts? Many calls come in from Muskoka, Georgian bay, lake Simcoe, to the Toronto life-saving crew for assistance. We also receive calls from Georgian bay and many points on lake Huron, and on lake Ontario and its rivers. Many members from maritime constituencies in Ontario know of the conditions that exist on our great lakes during the fall of the year. A situation exists that is not at all creditable to this country which calls itself a nation. Many of the men who serve on the ships that ply the great lakes are equal to those who fought at St. Julien, and yet these men on Canadian ships are forced to sound their sirens to call United States life-saving crews to come to their assistance when they are in danger in the late fall-a fine toast to Canadian nationhood. It is not fair to these men who are advancing our grain crop to' the seaboard by water to be without proper aids to navigation, and as one of the representatives of the city of Toronto I protest. I am sent here to find out something about this vote. The city of Toronto pays $96,000 a year to give a lifesaving service to the province. Calls come in from as far away as North Bay for this service; the city has sometimes to transport by flat car not only a life-saving boat but skilled men to handle it, and the service is maintained all the year around.

The minister is in charge of all the navigation laws of the country. You have a large number of steamers on the great lakes. There was a boat attached to Amherstburg near Windsor, which the captain had to run into a bank or twelve hundred people would have been drowned two years ago. At the entrance of the Niagara river, for instance, there is a large sand bar five or six miles long. I was on board the boat going to the Niagara camp with the 74th or the 75th battalion, and in a wind storm the ship ran right on this sand bar and was there for the best part of a day. If an accident happens, all you can do is to sound your whistle to get the Toronto life-saving station. The city of Toronto is providing this whole service for the province, and at a time when the government is taking revenues away from the municipalities. The sum of $100,000-that is what it is with summer beach extra protection-of the taxpayers' money of the city of Toronto has to be spent to maintain this service and train these men to act as a life-saving crew. That is something which the federal government should do of its own volition, because by the British North America Act navigation is a federal responsibility. We heard in a debate in this house the other day that human life is not

held sacred on the land; and on the water there is no chance at all. We have absolutely no life-saving station maintained by the federal government for the protection of the steamers or the merchant marine on the great lakes, and in case of accident all they have to depend upon is some life-preservers and a few old rowboats, and investigations that were conducted showed that the rowboats could not be got out in time, and that some crews received no proper drills. The time is coming, Mr. Chairman, when the municipalities cannot stand this any longer. Toronto has had to spend $51,000,000 on relief, and we should have relief from this item of $96,000 which the city of Toronto is spending on its life-saving service for the benefit of the province. I think this government should give Toronto $50,000 towards the work it is doing. The life-saving crew of the Toronto station has been called to many different places. In front of the summer cottage of one of my colleagues from Toronto who is not present at the moment there was an accident not long ago in which five or six people were in peril, and they had to send to the Toronto lifesaving station for dragging irons to get these poor people out.

Members of parliament have been criticized by a section of the press for being decadent, but I say that the House of Commons is no more decadent than the public press has been of recent years, and if there is no public press to bring this and other matters to the attention of the government, it is the duty of a private member of parliament to do it. That is why I am bringing it to the attention of the responsible minister who is administering this trust, and a very sacred trust it is. I would not want to travel on some of the boats that are under the control of the minister. There are two boats going to Port Dalhousie at the present time. I was on one of them once, and I would not say it is safe; I have not been on it again.

I did not know this item was coming up to-night or I could have read in detail what the Toronto life-saving station is doing. It is doing federal work. Navigation is under the exclusive jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada by the British North America Act. I do not object to the maritimes getting votes for navigation because they are entitled to them, and they have been getting only pin-money in many ways for a maritime province, but I do urge the minister to do something for the only modem life-saving station on the lakes at Toronto, and in Ontario and for aids to life-saving and navigation in the late

column2: COMMONS

fall. They are called all over the province. Look what is being done around the Detroit river! They call on the war department of the United States, which maintains large stations and fast boats on the lakes winter and summer, and I venture to say that the insurance on our Canadian ships in the fall of the year would be much greater if the insurance companies did not depend on the United States life-saving stations to do the duty which Canada should have done. It is a fine commentary on Canada being a nation and on the talk and chatter at banquets of such a claim while brave sailors are drowned!

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Langton Church,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac&Language=E&Section=ALL
1145545,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.76,1938-04-25,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Transport,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,My hon. friend is very fond of saying what Toronto does in life-saving. It is true that in Toronto harbour there are several fast motor boats that have to do with the safety of life in Toronto harbour, but their work is chiefly that of life-saving crews at beaches and attendants at swimming pools. Incidentally that is conducted not by the city of Toronto but by the Toronto harbour commission, which is responsible in a measure to the department we are now discussing.

I hold no great brief for the service provided by the Department of Transport, but I am tired of hearing so much about our great dependence upon the United States service, and how great a service it is. As a matter of fact, the worst marine disaster on the great lakes within two years occurred at the entrance to Cleveland harbour, when the Sand Merchant went down, and I did not hear of any great rescue there.

The fact of the matter is-and we recognize it in the department-that the service we are discussing was designed for the days of wooden ships, and to-day, with all the aids to navigation, with wireless and wireless telephone on the boats, the service is not the type of service that is of any particular merit as an aid in the protection of life on the great lakes. During the past year we have had an extensive study made of the whole situation, and the report, I am told, is about ready for us. It will mean in my opinion either that we abandon the service altogether or that we put in modern mechanized equipment which will be able to cope with the type of disaster which we have at the present time. But in the meantime the service we are maintaining is actually the same service that has been maintained for at least fifty years, and longer, I assume, in this dominion. All I can say is that when these estimates come up next year we shall have new recommendations to make concerning this item.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1145546,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.77,1938-04-25,b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac,ca.m.9274,Mr. CHURCH:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,I am surprised that the minister knows so little about the case of the city of Toronto. I was chairman of the board of control and one of the harbour commission when we took over this work in 1916, and I can tell the minister that the city of Toronto gives $96,000 to the harbour board for this particular work instead of the city doing the work itself. This $96,000 is the taxpayers' money of the city of Toronto, earmarked for this purpose. The harbour board have no revenue as such. The amount is $73,136 for 1938, but with extra work done it is $96,000. All the revenue they get comes from the city of Toronto, and this whole amount of $96,000 is paid by the taxpayers of the city of Toronto to its trustee board, the harbour board. That is the fact, and it cannot be disputed.

The minister need not.be sick and tired of hearing about Toronto. The city is also sick of the unjust treatment it receives. Toronto is entitled to a fair show from this house and from the minister. The minister need not be sick of Toronto. Toronto, I can tell the minister, is the largest tax-paying city in Canada, and this government is collecting $40,000,000 in income tax from that city, and in all $90,000,000 of revenue, while we get nothing. I am sick and tired of hearing the minister make statements like he did a moment ago when he said that it was not the city of Toronto but the harbour board that was paying the $96,000. What the minister said is not a fact. And he need not be sick of Toronto. The city of Toronto is sick of the kind of treatment it is getting from this department. Facilities are provided all over the country at the expense of the government; there are airports throughout the country so established. But in the case of Toronto the same treatment is not given. I do not like to bring these matters up; but when Toronto, the city I represent, is attacked by the minister, I am bound to reply. I want justice and fair dealing. I was sent here to represent that city, and I can tell the minister that Toronto is the only city which gave a grant in connection with a viaduct that cost $30,000,000. We have three or four mills of our tax rate for purely federal burdens.

The minister need not be sick of Toronto; he may be sick of me, but he will be far more sick later on if he continues along the line he is now going. I repeat, we are entitled to some consideration. The minister is a gentleman for whom I have a great deal of respect, and I tell him that the city of Toronto is not being fairly treated. The morgue in Toronto is full of outsiders; for whenever there is any drowning fatality life-saving crews are
Supply-Transport-Life Saving Service

sent out by the city all over central Ontario. They are sent to North Bay, Nipissing, lake Simcoe, Georgian bay, lake Huron, all over lake Ontario and to the lake Simcoe district ports. Why should the city pay for these federal services? Navigation and shipping and aids to navigation including life-saving are all, under the British North America Act, part of the duties and functions of the dominion government. I see my young friend the hon. member for Trinity here to-night. He goes out yachting sometimes and he knows something of the work of these life-saving crews. As a yachtsman he will agree with everything I say.

I do not wish to delay this vote; far from it; but I do want to see some protection provided for those using the ferry boat and the Niagara and other lake boats. One serious accident happened to a boat at Broekville the year before last. I want to see these people on the lakes given some protection, but under our present laws they have none. What is the 847,000 for? It is for temporary service, but I doubt whether one man will be saved as a result of it. Did the coastal trade get any of it? Did Hamilton, Cobourg and other cities and towns benefit? I do not see the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario here, but I know that up in Muskoka there are no life-saving stations. When anyone is drowned they have to telephone to Toronto for a crew with grappling irons and life-saving equipment. Well, if that is all the life-saving the department is doing, I can tell the minister that however sick he may be of Toronto he will be very much more sick at the next election, and will need all the life-savers he can get.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Langton Church,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b4773d7c-fb30-477a-9d14-c076e60905ac&Language=E&Section=ALL
1145547,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.78,1938-04-25,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,Is there not already in our law a provision by which all sea-going ships carrying passengers are inspected, (a) as to the boilers, and, (b) as to equipment, including life-saving apparatus, life-boats, life-rafts, and life-belts? That part of it, I understand, is in another vote and is cared for by the branch of the department formerly known as the Department of Marine and Fisheries. What the hon. member (Mr. Church) is dealing with is rather more important than the minister would indicate. He is dealing with the question of loss of life on the great lakes in ships that are not always subject to investigation and control by our own people, that is, ships which are cast up against the shores of our own country, sometimes with consequent loss of life. He has been suggesting that we should make provision for a fund to do the work which, unfortunately, he finds that the city of Toronto has to do at expense it can

ill afford. There is something in that argument. We should justly and fairly be required to make some financial provision for the safety of people and for the care of those who may be wrecked. But there has been at times, in all countries and under all circumstances, laxity in connection with inspection. The minister will recall the terrible disaster, with tremendous loss of life, that befell a certain ship which went out from New York. That tragedy occurred between New York and Cuba. There are other ships which I shall not mention by name, inasmuch as it might reflect upon the lines owning them. The same thing has happened on the great lakes. The minister referred to a ship that was not on the Canadian register.

1145551,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.82,1938-04-25,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,I thought she was on their register as well. I am in error as to that. As far as I could read, that ship had apparently been inspected. Was there any laxity in the matter of inspection, or was the accident one of the inevitable consequences of a storm or, shall I say, of an ill-directed course? Was there laxity in the inspection of her boilers and equipment and matters of that kind? That is the question to which the hon. member is directing attention, and properly so. The investigations into the accident that happened to the ship which was lost off the Atlantic coast between New York and Cuba, and the accident that overtook the United States vessel lost near Asbury Park, New Jersey, disclosed lack of discipline in one case, and in both cases some laxity in inspection. In connection with the Sand Merchant, was anything disclosed that indicated that we had failed in the discharge of our duty in the testing of boilers, equipment, lights and all the other factors that go to make up the safety of a ship? Was she certificated when she should not have been? Was she given a certificate of fitness which she should not have had? Those are proper questions, and I think the minister will agree that there is a duty cast upon the nation rather than upon municipal institutions to bear the cost that may be involved in connection with matters of this kind.

1145556,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.87,1938-04-25,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Transport,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,The court found that the loss of the Sand Merchant was due to the shifting of the cargo of sand, and that the loss of life must be laid to the first, and, to a lesser degree, the second officers, who were overconfident and not sufficiently alert in obeying the master's orders to get the life-boats out and the crew aboard. The court exonerates the master from blame but considers that he should be warned, and that he is open to censure for failing to have fife-boat drill aboard his vessel, and for permitting an unauthorized person to be on board. The operators of the vessel were held to be without blame.

,Liberal,,Clarence Decatur Howe,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb&Language=E&Section=ALL
1145557,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.88,1938-04-25,b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f,ca.m.6164,Mr. BENNETT:,Leader of the Official Opposition,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,It comes down perhaps to a question of proper stevedoring of the sand.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Richard Bedford Bennett,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=b9296f13-96f7-4c62-a577-63a5fc91ac2f&Language=E&Section=ALL
1145558,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.89,1938-04-25,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Transport,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,Yes; apparently they were too confident; they did not realize the roughness of the sea, and did not stow their sand properly. Of course the municipal bathing beaches are the responsibility of the municipalities. The Toronto harbour commission's expenses are paid in part by shipping. The commission looks after the safety of shipping, and the city contributes to the cost of lifeguards on the beaches and purely municipal services. However, as I said, this particular vote is to maintain life-boats and life-saving stations at certain points on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts and the great lakes. The type of equipment used, the service generally, is in our opinion not in tune with modern requirements. We have been studying the situation for some months, we hope to arrive at a conclusion which we can present to the committee when the estimates come up next year. It will mean either a largely increased vote or the abolition of the vote altogether. In other words we believe that the present service is very little better than no service at all, and unless we can find a way of putting on a first class service we may ask to abolish it.

1145562,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.93,1938-04-25,090c4da7-b949-45d0-b63f-39854ba32056,ca.m.2263,Mr. NEILL:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,I hope the minister does not indicate that he proposes to abolish the lifesaving service entirely on the Pacific coast. Reorganization might be necessary, but to do away with it would be a retrograde step. At present service is given on the west coast of Vancouver island by two life-saving stations operating small gasoline life-boats. It might be that some improvement could be made in the service. I have heard it suggested that it might be advantageous to put on a larger boat which would patrol the whole coast and be always on the water, with wireless equipment so as to be readily available at any point. To compensate to some extent for the increased cost it might be equipped so that, especially in summer time when the life-saving work would not be excessive, it could handle some minor duties, such as serving the lighthouses; because that work is always increasing. Hardly a month goes by that there is not a demand for another light somewhere, which all means additional work for the already overdriven tenders, the Estevan, and I think the Alberni, to serve these lighthouses. And there is the yearly replacement of the acetylene in the fixed lights, where there is no guardian at all, which might be done by a smaller boat as a sort of auxiliary. In that way it might be possible to relieve the pressure on the lighthouse service and still maintain the life-saving phase. It would be unfortunate if the minister undertook to abandon that.

The owner or occupier of every dock, wharf or landing place at which passengers are put on shore or taken on board, shall also, at night, cause to be shown conspicuously on such dock, wharf or landing place, at every angle or turn thereof, during the whole of the time that any such ship is approaching, or alongside, good and sufficient lights.

loss,
column2: from year to year, necessitating new contracts for the replacement of articles which in the usual course of affairs never wear out. 1145632,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.163,1938-04-25,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Transport,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,There are 700 buoys in the Montreal agency alone, on the St. Lawrence river and I suppose approximately the same number in the Quebec agency. We lose about forty a year, and the expense runs about an average of $10,000 a year. We do not deliberately try to lose them. Generally the buoys are sheered away by the ice. We have winter buoys all the way from Montreal harbour to below Quebec, which are required for the use of the ice-breakers. With the shifting ice, occasionally a buoy will be ripped away from its mooring chain.

column2: I know the minister is always careful with the equipment under his care, which after all is the property of the Canadian taxpayer, and he should be in a position to tell us exactly how these things occur. Who makes

column1: [Mr. Lockhart.)

the report? Who takes care of these things? They are worth money, and they should be considered by the department in exactly the same light as the Minister of Finance would consider the dollars under the control of his department. If the minister cares to go over the figures and give them to us later on, I am sure an opportunity will develop to tell the people exactly how these things are done. It may result in saving the Canadian taxpayer a vast amount of money now being spent for sinkers which in the ordinary course of events could not possibly wear out.

1145646,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.177,1938-04-25,0cd180b9-3a82-4810-b0ce-83bc28f5b7c5,ca.m.7237,Mr. ISNOR:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,I wonder if I would be in

order in asking the minister to revert to item No. 410? This item went through without any questions being asked, and I missed it when I went to my office to procure a memorandum. It appears to me that there is discrimination against the Atlantic coast in connection with these subsidies. A subsidy is paid to a company operating out of Quebec and to another company operating on the Pacific coast. Last year I suggested that in order to provide greater protection on the Atlantic coast a subsidy should be paid in connection with this particular work. There is a large salvage company operating out of Halifax, and I feel that they are under a handicap due to the fact that a subsidy of $30,000 is paid in one case and SI5.000 in another to salvage companies operating out of other ports. I should like the minister :o give to the committee the conditions under which these two companies operate and explain why these subsidies are paid.

very reason advanced by the minister that a handicap is placed on the company which is operating successfully out of Halifax. I am not advocating that the government should give the company in Halifax a subsidy; but if they can operate successfully, why cannot the company from Quebec stand on its own feet and operate on the same basis? I have known cases where the company from Quebec was obliged to steam 550 odd miles into territory covered by the company operating out of Halifax, and it would take the Quebec boat two and a half days to reach a certain point whereas the boat from Halifax could reach it in one and a half or two days at the most. I really cannot see why the subsidy should be paid to the Quebec company as against no subsidy on the Atlantic coast.

1145671,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.202,1938-04-25,4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8,ca.m.3404,Mr. MacNICOL:,,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,"Mr. Chairman, a year

ago I asked the minister if he was satisfied as an engineer that the method which had been followed by the department for several years, perhaps many years, of keeping the channel open was the correct way of doing this work. Every year we have an item in the estimates like this, or for double or treble the amount, or a similar item may appear in public works. So that over the years the dredging of the St. Lawrence ship channel has cost the country a vast sum of money.

Last summer when returning up the St. Lawrence I got up early in the morning ""o have a look at the channel as the ship went up the river. I went on the bridge, having first discussed the matter with the captain and having discussed with him the possibility of the methods that are being followed not being the very best to keep the channel as it should be. It appears that one year the harbour is deepened, and another year the outlets to the harbour are. Apparently what is done is to increase the flow of water out of lake St. Louis into the river. Is that the right way? The harbour continually recedes lower and lower, and as the harbour continues to recede naturally the following year the river has to be dredged again. The question is, where will it end? Are we following the right engineering methods? I am not prepared to say. Are
Supply
Transport-St. Lawrence Dredging
we following the same engineering methods that are followed in all large rivers such as the Elbe in Germany, the Rhine flowing into the North Sea and the Thames?

I have read of, as I am sure the minister has, and last summer I saw, the plans of a proposed dam across the Thames at London to eliminate this sort of thing, thereby maintaining the level of the water. Has any survey been made of any possible plans to eliminate every year the expenditure of four, five, or six million dollars, more or less in dredging Montreal harbour and east? Certainly anything that can be done to improve the harbour should be done. Anything that can be done to improve that great waterway, one of the greatest in the world, over which there floats more commerce than over a great many of the large rivers of the world, should be done, and I will support anything along that line to provide shipping facilities for the improvement of that harbour. As a Canadian, and like all other Canadians, I am proud of what has been done by this country to increase shipping facilities in that harbour. On the other hand, I am not so sure that we are following the best methods in our attempt to reduce the cost of maintaining those facilities. I asked the same question a year ago. I wonder whether in the meantime the minister has had an opportunity to make a survey in order to find out whether we are following the right methods in constantly dredging and digging the outlet of Montreal harbour, reducing the water level, instead of doing something to maintain it, and eliminating the constant necessity for spending millions in dredging.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,John Ritchie MacNicol,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4ec07e21-5e6c-41f8-9fa6-c6cbf37549e8&Language=E&Section=ALL
1145672,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.203,1938-04-25,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Transport,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,In January, 1934, the former government set up an interdepartmental Montreal ship channel water levels board to study this very question that my hon. friend has now brought up. The board spent over three years in making a thorough study of the requirements of the river. The desired result is of course a minimum depth of thirty-five feet at low tide, low water, and a width adequate for the largest type of boats to traverse safely from the ocean to Montreal. The board made a report some months ago. I have that report here and shall be glad to furnish my hon. friend with a copy of it. The decision was that a procedure more or less like that which had been followed is required to complete that work. The report goes into considerable detail with regard to the work required to complete the channel, and it is estimated that a cost of $11,500,000 will be required to obtain an adequate channel of the dimensions that I have just indicated.

Maintenance work on the St. Lawrence is in itself very light. There are only two or three points where silting occurs and where constant maintenance work is required. For a channel of that length, however, the maintenance work in itself is a fairly simple problem. In the actual construction of the channel the work has been going on for a great many years, and if the interdepartmental board is correct we are now approaching the end, so that in the next four or five years we can say to the world that we have a thirty-five foot channel of adequate width from the sea to Montreal; and this capital vote, if not dispensed with entirely, should be reduced to a very small amount.

1145701,ca.proc.d.1938-04-25.2.33.7.232,1938-04-25,1716566b-edef-40b2-9552-49510618c3bb,ca.m.9539,Mr. HOWE:,Minister of Transport,QUESTIONS,DEPARTMENT OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS,DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT,Just a moment; the hon. gentleman wanted the story of this transaction and I am giving it to him. As I say, part of the work of dredging the St. Lawrence consisted of maintaining a shipyard at Sorel for the repair of the government fleet, and the government fleet was an expensive unit. I believe there were some sixteen dredges, six tugs, several coal barges, a quantity of dump scows and the various auxiliary equipment that goes with dredging operations.

I think the Sorel shipyard has been a source of concern to every Minister of Marine who has anything to- do with it. The difficulty, of course, was that the shipyard was primarily built to repair one particular fleet of boats. The boats required overhaul in the winter months, and when they were operating they required only casual repairs. The shipyard's main work was to look after this dredging fleet. The result, of course, was that in order to maintain steady employment at the shipyard a number of men had to be maintained in idleness while the dredges were in operation. It is impossible to maintain an efficient operation under those circumstances. As a result of the idleness at the shipyard in the summer months it became a convenient depository for men for whom it was desirable to find employment. It has been estimated by my officers that an efficient crew at the shipyard would consist of about 250 men. The number actually employed fluctuated. I think it was never less than about four hundred even in my time; I never was able to get it below that, and it went as high as nine hundred and at times a thousand men. As a result we were appropriating something over S200,000 each year for the shipyard

generally, and in addition repairs to the dredges were charged against the dredging appropriation. My officers estimated that the repairs to the dredges could have been made at outside points for at least one-third less than the charges at the Sorel shipyard, and it must be remembered that the charges for the work done were in addition to the amount of over $200,000 appropriated each year for the shipyard itself.

So much for the Sorel shipyard. When I came into office the dredging fleet was only twenty-five per cent efficient; in other words, seventy-five per cent of the fleet was tied up or anchored in the stream, entirely useless except for scrap. The twenty-five per cent that we called efficient consisted of dredges of a type no longer efficient for working in a thirty-five foot channel. We had ladder dredges; one of them sank shortly after we sold them. I was afraid it would happen before we got rid of the fleet, but it was not our loss. It was the loss of the buyer; a case of caveat emptor, I think. At any rate we had equipment that was far from efficient for the purpose for which it was to be used. Analysis of the dredging costs indicated that forgetting all about the repair bill the cost of a yard of contract dredging was considerably less than the cost of a yard of dredging with our own crews and equipment. It was necessary for me to examine the situation to see what was to be done. Should we buy new equipment; should we repair the existing equipment.; should we attempt to modernize some of the dredges that we had, or should we dispose of the outfit and carry on by contract dredging? In arriving at a conclusion I had to keep in mind the report of the departmental board that about another eleven and a half million dollars of expenditure would complete the thirty-five foot channel for all time, except for small maintenance expenditures.

It seemed to me that the course was clear. If we carried on with the fleet we had, at the end of the eleven and a half million dollar program we would have a fleet and a shipyard with no work to be done. The capital cost of modernizing the equipment seemed out of proportion to the amount of work that equipment would have to do, for eleven and a half million dollars is not a very big program as dredging programs go. It seemed to me that we should dispose of that shipyard and dredging plant while we had a little leverage in the way of contract work to help the sale along. I took the responsibility as to procedure, and I might say that I had the advantage of some little background that I

thought entitled me to handle a transaction of that kind. All my life has been spent in the construction business, and the last twenty-five years have been spent in negotiating and awarding contracts having to do with the construction industry. I have considerable knowledge of dredging work, because from time to time during the period of my professional practice I have been associated with projects requiring a good deal of dredging. For that reason I took on the work of handling this transaction.

My first step was to obtain the valuation of the assets, and for that purpose I retained the Canadian Appraisal Company, the largest and, I believe, one of the most reliable appraisal companies in Canada, to make an appraisal of the property, comprising the dredging fleet and the shipyard, with the exception of such parts of the property as we decided to retain for maintenance purposes. An appraisal was made, and a valuation placed on each item.

I then considered where we could find a buyer. There were a good many problems in that connection, the chief one being the maintenance of labour. Naturally we had a large number of men employed at the Sorel shipyards, and a considerable number employed on the St. Lawrence fleet, and when seeking a buyer it was necessary to keep in mind the continuity of the employment of those men. The main contractor for dredging work on the St. Lawrence, since its inception, has been General Dredging Contractors Limited, with headquarters at Sorel. However, the work has been too large for any one firm, and this company has associated with it the Canadian Dredging and Dock Company and
J.
column2: P. Porter and Sons, Limited, the three companies I believe owning about two-thirds of all dredging equipment in Canada, and having the greater part of that dredging equipment engaged in the deepening work in the St. Lawrence river.

column1: It appeared to me that these were the only firms capable of undertaking a project of this size, or having equipment suitable to carry out the work. The fact that the General Dredging Contractors Limited had headquarters at Sorel, where the shipyard was located, and also operated a shipyard at that point which could merge with operation of the government plan, and work out a program for maintaining the level of employment in Sorel, indicated to me that General Dredging Contractors Limited were the people who should buy this property. I approached them on the subject and found them at first extremely reluctant to enter into the trans-
Supply-Transport-St. Lawrence Dredging
action. However, I was determined that this was the time to sell the property, and I urged them to consider the matter.

The negotiations extended over two or three months. Of course the appraisal made by the Canadian Appraisal Company was the basis for negotiations. Finally we arrived at a price which was about seventy-nine per cent of the value the Canadian Appraisal Company had put on the property. The leverage I used on the contractor to work out the contract was the fact that if this could be worked out we were in a position to award the balance of the dredging.

The method of awarding the dredging contract may be questioned. I believe that there again we used every safeguard and exercised the best business judgment. The first contract for dredging the St. Lawrence was awarded in 1930 to the lowest tenderers, tenders having been called for in 1929. The lowest tenderer had associated with him his two greatest competitors. So that the three principal dredging companies in Canada were working on the dredging of the St. Lawrence at prices which represented the lowest tender in 1929.

true valuation was placed on the equipment at the Sorel shipyards in 1936 because, as the minister says, it was the first inventory that had ever been reported to the auditor general. He accounted for $7,872,007.01 of this increase in the inventory I am talking about. The same thing happened in the Quebec agency, with the result that altogther there has been a vast increase in the amount of money represented in the holdings at the Sorel shipyards, the Quebec agency and the St. Lawrence ship channel.

But the question of valuation is only one part of the item under discussion this evening. The minister maintains that the true valuation is the one given to him by the Canadian Appraisal Company, and I say that just five months prior to that his own officers in his department for the first time made a valuation of certain properties which exceeded the valuation placed upon them by the Canadian Appraisal Company by something like ten million dollars. Inasmuch as this was the first time an inventory was taken, I would like the minister to explain just how that difference occurred. Surely it cannot be said that that amount of depreciation took place over a period of four months. Certainly that is hard to believe.

In order to show quite clearly that the Canadian Appraisal Company's valuation is not a true one, let me take simply the industrial site covered by the Sorel shipyards. I have under my hand a copy of the valuation placed on that particular property by the Canadian Appraisal Company, and I find that they appraise the land, including wharves, railway sidings, paving, fences and drainage at $60,000, and buildings and other structures at $125,789. In the town of Sorel we find that that property, though it does not produce any revenue, is carried on the assessment rolls at 81,000,000. Yet the Canadian Appraisal Company submitted an appraisal of something like $215,000 for property assessed approximately at $1,000,000.

Furthermore, let us consider the cost to the government of this land, in order to try to ascertain its true value. The Canadian government has purchased this land from various individuals and the records show how much has been paid for this land per square foot. It is almost eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman, and I have a good deal more to say.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
